assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Variation
items.clue: Differences in traits between individual organisms.

items.label: Speciation
items.clue: The splitting of one species into two or more species.

items.label: Interspecific hybrid
items.clue: An offspring produced when members of two different species breed.

items.label: Biological species concept
items.clue: The definition of a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes variation between organisms?

options.text: No two individuals are identical in all their traits, and the patterns of variation are the basis for classifying organisms.
Individuals produced by asexual reproduction share one genome and so are identical in all of their traits.
Organisms are classified by a single distinguishing trait, so variation in the other traits is not used in naming them.
Organisms that look markedly different from one another must be members of two different species.

questions.stem: How did Linnaeus define a species?

options.text: As a group that can breed to produce fertile offspring
As a group of organisms that can mate and have offspring
As a group of organisms that share a set of traits
As organisms that look identical in every trait

questions.explanation: Linnaeus used the original morphological concept: a species is a group of organisms with shared traits, which distinguish them from other groups. This remains the practical basis of identification.

questions.stem: Which statement about the scientific name of the tiger, Panthera tigris, is correct?

options.text: The second word, tigris, is on its own enough to identify the species of tiger.
It should be written Panthera Tigris, because both of its words are proper nouns.
Panthera tigris and Panthera leo are varieties of one species and interbreed freely.
Panthera names the genus and tigris distinguishes the species within it.

questions.explanation: In the binomial system the first part of the name identifies the genus and the second part distinguishes the species from other species in that genus. Panthera leo, the lion, shares the genus and has similar traits.

questions.stem: According to the biological species concept, what is a species?

options.text: A group of organisms that can mate and produce offspring of any kind
A group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring
A group of organisms that resemble one another in every visible trait
A group of organisms that live in the same area and interbreed with one another

questions.explanation: The biological species concept defines a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring. Fertility of the offspring is the decisive condition.

questions.stem: Which statement about speciation is correct?

options.text: It is the splitting of one species into two or more, usually happening gradually as populations become more different.
It occurs at the moment when a single mutation produces the first individual of a new species.
It ends at a definite point that can be identified by testing whether the populations are separate.
It is complete as soon as a population becomes geographically separated from the rest of its species.

questions.stem: Which statement about chromosome numbers is correct?

options.text: Humans must have more chromosomes than chimpanzees, because humans are the more complex and advanced organism.
Human diploid cells have 46 chromosomes, chimpanzee diploid cells have 48, and diploid numbers are even.
Human body cells contain 23 chromosomes in total, which is why a diploid number can be an odd number.
Chromosome number determines genome size, so 48 chromosomes must contain more DNA than 46.

questions.stem: Which set of features is used to classify the chromosomes when a karyogram is prepared?

options.text: Length only, so that chromosomes of equal size are matched into pairs
Number of genes and total amount of DNA in each chromosome
Base sequence differences, seen directly as bands on the chromosome
Length, position of the centromere, and banding pattern

questions.explanation: Chromosomes in a karyogram are classified by their length, by the position of the centromere, which sets the relative lengths of the two arms, and by the pattern of bands produced by staining.

questions.stem: What is meant by the genome of an organism?

options.text: The set of genes that is identical in every member of the organism's species
The number of chromosomes in each of the organism's diploid body cells
All of the genetic information of the organism, including non-coding DNA
The genes whose base sequences determine all of the proteins the organism makes

questions.explanation: The genome is all the genetic information of an organism: the whole base sequence of its DNA, coding and non-coding, in the nucleus and in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Members of a species share most of their genome.

questions.stem: Which statement about whole genome sequencing is correct?

options.text: Sequencing a single complete human genome still takes several years and costs many hundreds of millions of dollars.
Its cost has fallen and its speed has increased, and it is used in research into evolutionary relationships.
It is used routinely to tell each patient exactly which diseases they will develop and when.
It has shown that two humans differ from each other by more than a human differs from a chimpanzee.

questions.stem: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. What can be concluded from these names alone?

options.text: Lions and tigers are two distinct species with similar traits that are classified together in the genus Panthera.
Lions and tigers are two varieties of a single species, Panthera, that interbreed freely in the wild.
Each species is named by its second word alone, so the shared first word carries no information about them.
Lions and tigers look so different that they cannot be closely related enough to be placed in the same genus.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell

questions.explanation: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.stem: Which is a correct comparison of bacteriophage lambda and HIV?

options.text: Both have an icosahedral head joined to a tail through which the genetic material is injected.
Both carry reverse transcriptase so that their genetic material can be copied into DNA.
Lambda has double-stranded DNA and no envelope, whereas HIV has RNA and an envelope.
Both have a capsid made of phospholipid taken from the membrane of the host cell.

questions.stem: In the lytic cycle of bacteriophage lambda, what happens after the phage has attached to a receptor on the surface of an E. coli cell?

options.text: The whole phage is taken into the cell and the capsid is broken down in the cytoplasm.
The phage DNA passes through the tail into the cell, and the capsid remains outside it.
The phage membrane fuses with the bacterial membrane, releasing the DNA inside.
The phage releases its ribosomes and enzymes into the cell to begin making phage proteins.

questions.stem: What happens to the DNA of bacteriophage lambda in the lysogenic cycle?

options.text: It is integrated into the host chromosome and is copied along with it.
It stays as a separate circle in the cytoplasm, like a plasmid, replicating on its own.
It is transcribed slowly, making a few phages that leave the cell without lysis.
It is permanently inactivated, so the cell and its descendants can no longer make phages.

questions.explanation: In lysogeny the lambda DNA is integrated into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage. It is replicated with the chromosome at each cell division and inherited by both daughter cells, while the genes for the lytic cycle are kept switched off.

questions.stem: Why do influenza viruses and HIV evolve so rapidly?

options.text: Their genome-copying enzymes lack proofreading, and vast numbers of virions are produced quickly.
Their RNA genomes are chemically unstable, so bases change spontaneously between one infection and the next.
They alter their genes deliberately whenever they are attacked by antibodies or by antiviral drugs.
They divide in two every few minutes, as bacteria do, so mutations accumulate over many divisions.

questions.stem: A student is constructing a dichotomous key to identify five species of tree growing in a local park. Which first step is the best design?

options.text: 1a Tree more than 10 m tall, go to 2; 1b Tree less than 10 m tall, go to 4
1a Leaves arranged in opposite pairs, go to 2; 1b Leaves arranged alternately, go to 4
1a Leaves needle-like, species A; 1b Leaves broad, species B; 1c Leaves scaly, species C
1a Grows in the damp part of the park, go to 2; 1b Grows in the dry part, go to 4
